title: On Pair Programming
summary: Thoughtworks guide to pair programming: styles, benefits (knowledge sharing, on-the-go review, WIP limits, onboarding) and challenges (exhaustion, power dynamics, junior confidence); argues review is not a substitute and that pairing cannot be proven scientifically.

assertions.quote: Having two people work on a piece of the code helps the team spread knowledge on technology and domain on a daily basis
When we pair, we have 4 eyes on the little and the bigger things as we go, more errors will get caught
In our experience, that is not sustainable. First of all it is just too exhausting.

verdicts.note: Self-reported fatigue is consistent across pairing studies; no measured limit.

A case study found that working 40 hours a week in pairs requires so much concentration that developers became exhausted, and the review's synthesis repeats that several developers regard pairing as exhausting; another project drifted back to solo programming toward its end.

assertions.quote: We disagree that code reviews are a good enough alternative to pairing.

verdicts.note: Microsoft studies show reviews catch fewer defects than expected, but head-to-head comparisons with pairing are lacking.

assertions.quote: junior programmers can also experience a loss of confidence in their own abilities when pairing

verdicts.note: Plausible and reported, though novice studies mostly show pairing helps juniors.

assertions.quote: One person is dominating the pairing session by hogging the keyboard and not giving room to their pairing partner.

verdicts.note: Qualitative studies document the dynamic; its effect on outcomes is unmeasured.

assertions.quote: pair programming limits the number of things a team can work on in parallel, and therefore increases the overall focus

verdicts.note: WIP limits improve flow in Kanban studies; attributing that to pairing is inference.

assertions.quote: Staunch opponents of pairing will always find ways to poke holes into the reproducibility

verdicts.note: The review describes research on particular practices like pair programming as at an intermediate or even mature state, and cites an earlier review calling pair programming supported by a well-established research stream; the evidence may be mixed, but the authors treat it as a scientifically studiable question, not an unmeasurable one.

Controlled experiments do measure pairing's effects on quality, duration and effort, but the meta-analysis concludes that 'is pairing better' has no single answer: it depends on programmer expertise and task complexity, so the value is measurable yet context-bound rather than unprovable.

assertions.quote: rote tasks might be a smell for bad design: Pairing can help you find the right abstraction for that boring code
